full_text:
Sheikh Aktaruneesa and B. Sarojini taking rest after casting their votes, at a polling station at the Montessori College of Physiotherapy in Vijayawada on Sunday.
| Photo Credit: Special arrangement
The sun blazed on Vijayawada on the polling day on Sunday, right from 9 a.m. Nonetheless, it did not deter elderly persons from exercising their voting right in the Second Ordinary Elections to Urban Local Bodies. The city recorded a maximum temperature of 33 degrees Celsius in the noon.
Many elderly persons, assisted by NSS volunteers and family members, reached the polling stations at Andhra Loyola College in the city to cast their vote.
At the polling station at the Montessori College Of Physiotherapy near Labbipeta, a 80-year-old woman, named B. Sarojini, walked alone in the sizzling heat from her house, located around 500 metres away, to the polling booth. Her children have deserted her, she says, and lives on ₹4,000 per month old-age pension.
Another 68-year-old woman, Sheik Aktarunneesa, who looked weaker than Sarojini, came by a share auto from One Town, around 5 km away, to cast her vote. She lost her elder son in an accident, and younger in a scuffle, and is deserted by her daughter-in-law and three daughters.
She came from Hyderabad where she stays with her fourth and widowed younger daughter. The pension is the only source of income for her, from which she supports her daughter as well, she says.

title: Heatwave: Pregnant women, children require extra protection — Experts - Punch Newspapers

As El Niño-linked heatwaves intensify, maternal and child health experts have urged pregnant women and parents to take extra precautions to protect themselves and their children from the extreme heat.
They explained that pregnant women and young children were particularly vulnerable to heat-related illnesses because of their physiological needs and limited ability to regulate body temperature.
The experts said excessive heat could increase fluid loss through sweating and raise the risk of dehydration, heat exhaustion and heatstroke, with potentially serious consequences for pregnant women and developing babies.
They also warned that children could become dehydrated more quickly than adults, particularly when they engage in outdoor activities or remain in poorly ventilated environments for extended periods.
The experts stated this while speaking on extreme heat associated with the El Niño weather phenomenon and protective measures to protect pregnant women and children.
PUNCH Healthwise reports that the Climate Impact Lab has warned that Nigeria could record an additional 31,400 heat-related deaths between September 2026 and February 2027 as an unusually strong El Niño weather pattern intensifies.
The projection places Nigeria among the countries expected to suffer the highest number of additional heat-related deaths globally during the six months, with nearly half of the 66,800 deaths projected across the Sahel region expected to occur in the country.
PUNCH Healthwise reports that amid the heat wave, the country also grapples with power shortages, with many homes lacking adequate cooling options.
The researchers project that global land temperatures will be 1.2 degrees Celsius above normal in the coming months, with 44 per cent more extremely hot days than would typically be expected.
Speaking exclusively to PUNCH Healthwise, a Consultant Obstetrician and Gynaecologist at the Federal Medical Centre, Abeokuta, Ogun State, Dr Olanrewaju Jimoh, said prolonged exposure to excessive heat could cause hypertension, heat stroke, and hormonal changes in expectant mothers and also expose their unborn babies to the risks.
He advised pregnant women to drink more water to avoid dehydration and associated risks such as stillbirth and preterm birth.
The consultant gynaecologist also advised pregnant women to avoid exposure to hot weather and wear loose and light-coloured clothing.
He listed congenital abnormalities, miscarriages, reduced placental blood flow, premature labour, and low birth weight, among others, as effects of extreme heat on the developing foetus in pregnant women.
“Severe heat stress at any stage—first, second, or third trimester—can trigger miscarriages or stillbirths,” he said.
Jimoh said extreme heat may worsen high blood pressure (gestational hypertension/preeclampsia) and gestational diabetes in pregnant women.
He said, “Pregnant women should go to the hospital immediately if they experience any of the following warning signs: Body temperature rising to 38.5°C or higher, high fever accompanied by red skin, confusion, fainting, or severe anxiety.
“Also, if they do not urinate for 8 hours or more or notice reduced or absent fetal movements, severe, persistent headache, or visual disturbances, persistent, unmanageable vomiting, sudden fluid leakage or drainage from the vagina, they should seek prompt medical help.”
To reduce the risks, the expert advised pregnant women to drink adequate water, avoid strenuous outdoor activities during peak heat periods, and stay in cool, well-ventilated spaces.
“They should drink at least 3 to 4 liters of fluid per day, and they should strictly avoid sugary juices, carbonated drinks, alcohol, caffeinated drinks, and energy drinks. Those with high blood pressure must strictly limit salt. They should eat water-rich fruits and vegetables such as watermelon, cucumber, and oranges, which help sustain body hydration.
“If going outside is necessary, they should use a large hat or an umbrella. Pregnant women should wear light, breathable cotton clothing and avoid heavy attire, suits, sweaters, or tight synthetic nightwear. They should take showers at least twice daily and use fans or air conditioning continuously,” Jimoh said.
Also speaking, a consultant paediatrician, Dr. Ayodele Renner, said extreme heat can affect children in many ways, urging parents and caregivers to pay attention to excessive thirst in children, particularly under five.
“Extreme heat affects children in various ways. First, the problem is that it increases their rate of insensible body water loss. With extreme temperatures, children can develop what we call heatstroke, in which an individual’s body temperature rises to levels that do not allow normal metabolism to take place.
“When metabolic processes begin to malfunction, children can experience various complications, including loss of consciousness, convulsions, and electrolyte problems, such as high levels of sodium and various other electrolyte imbalances, which can lead to potentially fatal outcomes. This is particularly concerning for children under five, who depend on others for their fluid intake,” he said.
He urged parents and caregivers to invest in cooling systems like air conditioning, rechargeable fans, among others.
“Parents should keep their child or children as cool as possible and invest in a rechargeable fan. It is important for them to be kept cool and well hydrated to prevent the complications of these extreme temperatures.
The child health expert explained that water remains the best option for keeping children hydrated during a heatwave, urging parents to avoid serving them sugary drinks.
“Water is the best option, and one should generally avoid processed drinks and packaged drinks, such as sodas and packaged fruit juice. If one is giving anything sweetened, it is preferable that it should be freshly squeezed juice or cold-pressed juice.
“If one does not have access to that, then water really is the best. Fruits like watermelon are very hydrating and refreshing. When they are consumed cold, they not only offer hydration but also provide some degree of comfort,” he said.
Renner added, “Also, make sure that their clothing is minimal. Now is not the time to overwrap children. Now is the time to keep the child from sweating.”

title: Cyclone ‘Murasu’: Telangana issues orange alert for 6 districts amid heavy rainfall warning on Nov 2 - Livemint

full_text:
The Cyclonic Storm 'Murasu' is likely to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm by Monday morning (November 2) and is expected to cross the South Andhra Pradesh coast between Nellore and Narsapur around midnight on November 2, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has said.
The weather system looming over the Bay of Bengal comes days after Cyclone Arnab made landfall near Andhra Pradesh and Odisha on October 28.
The storm is likely to move towards the west-central Bay of Bengal and may bring rain to Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Tamil Nadu and Telangana.
"Cyclone 'Murasu' (war drum), named by India, is "set to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm and cross the land in Andhra Pradesh coast with wind speeds of 100-110 kmph gusting to 120 kmph between Nellore and Narsapur by morning of November 3," IMD said in latest bulletin.
Rainfall alert in Telangana: Check full forecast
The Meteorological Centre, Hyderabad, has issued orange and yellow alerts for several districts in the southern region for November 2.
An orange alert warning of heavy rainfall has been sounded for isolated places in Khammam, Nalgonda, Suryapet, Mahabubnagar, Nagarkurnool and Wanaparthy districts of Telangana.
A yellow alert has been issued for Jangaon, Yadadri Bhuvanagiri, Rangareddy, Hyderabad and Medchal-Malkajgiri districts of Telangana.
Thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and gusty winds of 30-40 kmph are very likely at isolated places in Khammam, Nalgonda, Siddipet, Yadadri Bhuvanagiri, Rangareddy, Hyderabad, Medchal-Malkajigiri, Mahabubnagar, Nagarkurnool, Wanaparthy, Suryapet, Mahabubabad, Warangal, Hanamkonda, Jangaon, Vikarabad, Sangareddy, Medak, Kamareddy, Narayanpet and Jogulamba Gadwal districts of Telangana.
Odisha has been put on high alert, prompting the state government to step up preparedness in the state.
Director of the Meteorological Centre, Bhubaneswar, Manorama Mohanty, said Odisha will receive rainfall from November 2, with the intensity of rain expected to increase on November 3 and 4 under the influence of the cyclone.
IMD predicts heavy rainfall | Full weather alert
The IMD said on Saturday that, under the influence of the system, isolated extremely heavy rainfall is likely over Coastal Andhra Pradesh and Yanam on November 2, followed by isolated very heavy rainfall on November 3. Isolated very heavy rainfall is also likely over Rayalaseema on November 2 and 3, and over Odisha on November 3 and 4, 2026.
Isolated heavy rainfall is likely over Arunachal Pradesh on November 1 and 2. The IMD also predicted isolated heavy rainfall in parts of Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal, and Telangana on November 2 and 3; in Kerala and Mahe from November 1 to 4; and over Coastal and North Interior Karnataka on November 3.

title: Cyclone Murasu: Five Odisha districts under orange alert for heavy rain - OrissaPOST

full_text:
Bhubaneswar: Five districts in southern Odisha have been placed under an orange warning for November 3 and 4 as Cyclonic Storm ‘Murasu’ moves towards the southern Andhra Pradesh coast, raising the possibility of heavy to very heavy rainfall in parts of the state.
Although the cyclonic system is not expected to make a direct impact on Odisha, its influence is likely to trigger rainfall, thunderstorms and gusty winds across several districts over the next few days, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD).
The weather office has forecast wind speeds of 50-60 kmph, with gusts reaching 70 kmph, in the five districts under the orange warning.
Rayagada, Koraput and Malkangiri are among the southern districts likely to experience the impact of the system.
Meanwhile, the Regional Meteorological Centre in Bhubaneswar has issued a yellow warning for thunderstorms and rainfall in 16 districts Sunday.
For Monday, Ganjam and Gajapati are under a warning for heavy rainfall, while other districts are likely to experience thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds of 30-50 kmph.
The weather is expected to remain unsettled as the cyclonic system develops over the Bay of Bengal and advances towards the Andhra Pradesh coast.
